title: The Conservative Case for International Law
gist: Two conservative writers argue, against the Trump administration's framing of the ICC as a sovereignty threat, that the U.S. right has a historical tradition (Taft, Root, Metternich) of embracing 'horizontal' international law among states as a bulwark against a 'law of the jungle,' and that the administration's Greenland, Venezuela, and Cuba actions exemplify exactly the predatory realism that tradition sought to prevent.

insights.claim: A recent poll found 49 percent of Americans believe the U.S. should arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if he travels to the U.S. for the UN General Assembly, versus 27 percent opposed, following NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's public call for his arrest and for the U.S. to join the ICC to execute its warrant.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Nearly half of U.S. public opinion now favors arresting a sitting Israeli PM on U.S. soil — a domestic political data point relevant to gauging future U.S. bipartisan support for unconditional Israel backing.
insights.quote: I believe that Prime Minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague
insights.locator: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made waves in July

insights.claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio characterized the ICC as waging 'a war' against the United States 'with statutes and compacts,' while President Trump stated 'I don't need international law' following the U.S. seizure of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Establishes the current administration's explicit rejection of international legal constraints on executive action abroad — a baseline for assessing sovereign/political risk in any country where the U.S. asserts extraterritorial interests.
insights.quote: the ICC and its friends are waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles, but with statutes and compacts and the force of so-called international law
insights.locator: Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned in a recent video message

insights.claim: Sen. Robert Taft ('Mr. Republican'), despite unimpeachable mid-century GOP credentials, argued in a 1949 speech opposing the North Atlantic Treaty that binding international law enforced by a veto-proof international court was the only real hope for preventing a third world war.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Provides historical precedent the authors use to argue that hostility to binding international law is a recent conservative development, not a longstanding one — relevant context for handicapping any future post-Trump GOP foreign-policy reset.
insights.quote: there is only one real hope of peace in the world to come—an association of nations binding itself to abide by a law governing nations and administered by a court of legal justice
insights.locator: As he argued in a 1949 speech opposing the North Atlantic Treaty

insights.claim: Elihu Root, who led the U.S. War and State Departments under Theodore Roosevelt, called the protection of international law 'the most valuable possession of all peaceable nations' in a 1915 speech as World War I killed off a generation of European men; even Metternich adopted 'Kraft im Recht' ('strength in law') as his motto.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Reinforces the historical-precedent argument with a foreign-policy realist (Metternich) explicitly endorsing legal constraint — undercuts the modern conflation of 'realism' with lawlessness.
insights.quote: Next to the preservation of national character, the most valuable possession of all peaceable nations, great and small, is the protection of those laws
insights.locator: Elihu Root—who helmed the War and State Departments

insights.claim: The authors distinguish 'law among states' — horizontal, procedural, supporting pluralism, trade, and conflict-containment (rooted in Hugo Grotius's 17th-century jus gentium) — from 'law over states' — vertical, purposive, and homogenizing, exemplified by the post-1945 'responsibility to protect' doctrine derived from Francis Deng's 'sovereignty as responsibility' concept, which lets non-state actors' claims chip away at state sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: A reusable framework for classifying any international-law or human-rights initiative as either sovereignty-respecting (likely to gain broad conservative and realist support) or sovereignty-eroding (likely to face conservative backlash) — useful for forecasting U.S. political reaction to future UN/ICC actions.
insights.locator: There are, then, two types of international law.

insights.claim: IR theorist Hedley Bull warned five decades ago that carried to its logical extreme, the doctrine of human rights under international law is subversive of the entire principle that mankind should be organized as a society of sovereign states, opening the door to a 'cosmopolitan community' replacing state sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Articulates the intellectual core of sovereigntist objections to expansive human-rights law — a lens for understanding why the ICC's 'responsibility to protect'-style jurisdiction draws bipartisan U.S. skepticism, not just Trump-era hostility.
insights.quote: Carried to its logical extreme, the doctrine of human rights and duties under international law is subversive of the whole principle that mankind should be organized as a society of sovereign states
insights.locator: As the great IR theorist Hedley Bull noted five decades ago

insights.claim: The authors characterize the Trump administration's foreign policy as 'flexible realism' that in practice functions as simple predation, citing the threatened seizure of Greenland from a treaty ally on a 'baseless pretext,' the seizure of Venezuela's leader and claims on its oil, and the effort to starve Cuba into regime change.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Frames a specific pattern (Greenland, Venezuela, Cuba) as evidence of a coherent U.S. policy of resource/territory coercion in the Western Hemisphere — a risk factor for any ally or neighbor with contested assets the U.S. administration might covet.
insights.locator: Witness the so-called flexible realism promulgated by the Trump administration.

insights.claim: The authors argue the Iraq and Iran wars — 'the two most egregious disasters of recent U.S. foreign policy' — could not have been launched by administrations that took international law seriously, implying that legal constraint functions as a practical check against costly, discretionary wars.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: A causal claim linking disregard for international law to specific costly U.S. military overreaches — relevant framework for assessing the probability and containment of future discretionary U.S. military action.
insights.locator: Indeed, it is no coincidence that the two most egregious disasters

themes.theme: A path forward on the ICC

insights.claim: The authors argue the ICC, while imperfect and shaped by the human-rights-centric 'law over states' vision they critique, is still 'better than nothing,' and that reform of the existing institution is easier than building a new one from scratch.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Suggests a plausible post-Trump conservative policy path is ICC reform/engagement rather than continued boycott — worth watching for shifts in U.S. ICC posture after 2028.
insights.locator: While it is possible to have international law without a world court

insights.claim: The authors argue that Netanyahu's war-crimes charges — 'starvation as a method of warfare' and intentionally targeting civilians — are crimes under traditional international law (the Geneva Conventions and UN Charter, both of which the U.S. is party to) regardless of whether the ICC exists or whether the U.S. has acceded to the Rome Statute.
insights.speaker: Luke Nicastro, Heather Penatzer
insights.so_what: Establishes that U.S. legal obligations toward alleged war crimes exist independent of ICC membership, meaning U.S. non-accession to the Rome Statute does not by itself insulate U.S. allies from accountability exposure under treaties Washington has actually signed.
